I'm noting that the error rate actually dipped slightly rather than rising, so the real impact was latency, not failures—and the "0.03 hours" figure refers to response time, not outage duration. The actual outage window was 07:39–07:45 (about 6 minutes), with recovery lining up with the 07:44:55 rollback and confirmation at 07:46:08, alongside p50 latency figures around 26ms.

The 183-192ms range comes from the investigator's hypothesis rather than something independently confirmed in the metrics, and the cause itself is only tied to timing correlation plus the rollback's success—not fully verified. I'm also flagging that the ClientDisconnected errors existed before the deploy, so they're baseline noise rather than something new. I should present these as observations rather than computed facts.

assumptions: The incident is treated as lasting from 07:39 to 07:45 UTC, the window in which the metrics show the service degraded. The separate, shorter figure for how long Argus held the incident open (until 07:46:08) measures response speed, not how long the service was broken, and is not used as an impact figure anywhere here.

Customer impact is characterised as latency, not errors: the error rate during the window was slightly below the pre-incident baseline, so no requests are attributed as having failed because of this incident despite a 2.0% momentary peak.

The specific latency figures cited in the investigation (p50 ~26ms rising to ~183-192ms) come from the Investigator Agent's hypothesis text rather than from a figure independently restated here; they are reported as the investigator's reading of the metrics.

Recovery is attributed to the rollback because the service returned to baseline immediately after it, but the metrics-recovery timestamp (07:45) is one minute earlier than the rollback confirmation (07:46:08), so the two are correlated rather than strictly proven cause and effect.
The recurring 'ClientDisconnected' account-page errors appear in the logs from 07:36, before the deploy, and are assumed to be pre-existing background noise unrelated to the cache misconfiguration.
The alternative hypothesis — that the io-summary-cache dependency itself failed — was never tested, since the rollback resolved the symptom; it is assumed ruled out rather than disproven.
No feature-flag changes were involved; the flag provider's history showed none in the relevant period.
input.executive_summary: On 28 September 2026 a routine configuration change to the shop service pointed it at the wrong address for one of its internal caches. From 07:39 to 07:45 UTC — about six minutes — the service could not reach that cache, and pages that depend on it became markedly slower to load for customers. Requests still succeeded: the share of failing requests over the window was no higher than the level seen just before the incident, so this was a slowdown rather than an outage, and no customer data or transactions were lost. An automated alert fired at 07:44, the offending change was rolled back within a minute of investigation completing, and the service was confirmed back to its normal behaviour shortly afterwards. A draft pull request has been opened to correct the configuration so the same change cannot be reapplied.
input.root_cause: The 07:39 production deploy of io-shop changed the io-summary-cache port in values-production.yaml from 6379 to 6380, a port the redis cache does not listen on, so every summary-cache lookup failed with "connection refused" and requests blocked on and retried the dead connection, driving latency well above baseline until the deploy was rolled back. Causation rests on the deploy timestamp matching the onset minute exactly, the refused-connection logs naming the changed port, and latency returning to baseline after rollback; no separate config diff verification was performed during the incident.
